This is a map of complexes and we denote the induced map on cohomology equally by
\underset{M_{\alpha}}{\smile}
.

It follows from the definition of
\mu^{2}_{M_{\alpha}}
that the cup product above extends the cup product of ordinary Hochschild cochains
\smile:C_{*}(A,A)\otimes C_{*}(A,A)\to C_{*}(A,A)
.

Proposition 5.7
.

The cohomology cup product
\underset{M_{\alpha}}{\smile}:HH^{*}(A,M_{\alpha})\otimes HH^{*}(A,M_{\alpha})\to HH^{*}(A,M_{\alpha})
is associative.

Proof.

The homotopy between the corresponding diagrams follows from the existence of
\mu^{3}_{M_{\alpha}}
and the equation it satisfies together with
\mu^{2}_{M_{\alpha}}
.
∎

In general, this cup product is not commutative, but it does satisfy the following compatibility with the product
\pi_{M_{\alpha}}
in
Definition

5.4
expressed in terms of the map of complexes

g^{M_{\alpha}}_{\alpha}:C_{*}(A,M_{\alpha})\to C^{*}(A,M_{\alpha})[n]

constructed in
Example

2.5
. For simplicity, we write
g^{M_{\alpha}}_{\alpha}
as
g_{\alpha}
below.

Proposition 5.8
.

There is a chain homotopy

g_{\alpha}(\pi_{M_{\alpha}}(-,-))\simeq g_{\alpha}(-)\underset{M_{\alpha}}{\smile}g_{\alpha}(-)

of maps of complexes
C_{*}(A,M_{\alpha})\otimes C_{*}(A,M_{\alpha})\to C^{*}(A,M_{\alpha})[-2n]
. The induced map

HH_{*}(A,M_{\alpha})\otimes HH_{*}(A,M_{\alpha})\to HH^{*}(A,M_{\alpha})[2n]

is
(-1)^{n}
-commutative.

Proof.

To prove the first assertion, we must write both sides as maps

C^{*}_{(2)}(A)\otimes C^{*}_{(2)}(A)\otimes C_{*}(A,M_{\alpha})\otimes C_{*}(A,M_{\alpha})\to C^{*}(A,M_{\alpha})

given by ribbon quivers (where we input
\alpha\otimes\alpha
into the first two factors) and find a homotopy between them. For the
(-1)^{n}
-commutativity, similarly we write the two ribbon quivers and find a homotopy that swaps the two inputs; comparing orientations at the end, we get the correct
(-1)^{n}
sign. We present both of these homotopies in
Section

A.4.2
.
∎

Recall from Remark
2.12
that if
\alpha
is non-degenerate, for any bimodule
M
the map

g_{\alpha}^{M}:C_{*}(A,M)\to C^{*}(A,M)[n]

is a quasi-isomorphism. Together with the previous proposition, this implies the following.

Corollary 5.9
.

If
\alpha
is non-degenerate, both the homology product
\pi_{M_{\alpha}}
and the cohomology cup product
\underset{M_{\alpha}}{\smile}
are
(-1)^{n}
-commutative.

5.2.2.
Relation to the categorical formal punctured neighborhood of infinity

We will now study the relation between the ‘cone bimodule’
M_{\alpha}
of
Definition

5.2
, defined using
\alpha
, and the bimodule
\widehat{A}_{\infty}
, whose definition is independent of
\alpha
.

Consider the map of
A
-bimodules given by the composition

A\otimes^{\mathbb{L}}_{A}A^{\vee}\xrightarrow{\sim}C_{*}(A,A^{\vee}\otimes A)\xrightarrow{g_{\alpha}^{A^{\vee}\otimes A}}C^{*}(A,A^{\vee}\otimes A)[n]

We also have another map of
A
-bimodules

A\otimes^{\mathbb{L}}_{A}A^{\vee}[-n]\xrightarrow{\sim}A^{\vee}[-n]\xrightarrow{f_{\alpha}}A

Together with the map defining
\widehat{A}_{\infty}
and the canonical map
A\to C^{*}(A,\mathop{\mathrm{Hom}}\nolimits_{\Bbbk}(A,A))
(which is always a quasi-isomorphism), these maps form a square

\textstyle{A\otimes^{\mathbb{L}}_{A}A^{\vee}[-n]\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\textstyle{A\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\textstyle{C^{*}(A,A^{\vee}\otimes A)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\textstyle{C^{*}(A,\mathop{\mathrm{Hom}}\nolimits_{\Bbbk}(A,A))}

Proposition 5.10
.

There is a homotopy making the square above commute, and defining a map of bimodules
M_{\alpha}\to\widehat{A}_{\infty}
. When
\alpha
is non-degenerate, this map is a quasi-isomorphism of bimodules.

Proof.

Again, for the first claim we write the ribbon quivers giving the two maps and a homotopy between them, in
Section

A.5
. The second claim follows from the fact (see
Remark

2.12
) that if
\alpha
is non-degenerate then
g_{\alpha}^{A^{\vee}\otimes A}
is a quasi-isomorphism (and thus the vertical maps are both quasi-isomorphisms).
∎

A quasi-isomorphism
M_{\alpha}\simeq\widehat{A}_{\infty}
of bimodules induces a quasi-isomorphism
C_{*}(A,M_{\alpha})\simeq C_{*}(A,\widehat{A}_{\infty})
. Combining this with the previous results of this section we have:

Theorem 5.11
.

Given a 4-truncated non-degenerate
n
-pre-CY category
(A,m)
, there is a product
\pi_{\infty}
on
HH_{*}(A,\widehat{A}_{\infty})[-n]
and a cup product
\underset{\infty}{\smile}
on
HH^{*}(A,\widehat{A}_{\infty})
, both associative and
(-1)^{n}
-commutative, related by
g^{\widehat{A}_{\infty}}_{\alpha}(\pi_{\infty}(-,-))=g^{\widehat{A}_{\infty}}_{\alpha}(-)\underset{\infty}{\smile}g^{\widehat{A}_{\infty}}_{\alpha}(-)
.

Remark 5.12
.

One could obtain a chain-level description of these operations by using the explicit quasi-isomorphism
M_{\alpha}\simeq\widehat{A}_{\infty}
and picking an inverse, but the resulting calculations would be rather complicated. We take the point of view that it is simpler to just use
M_{\alpha}
instead.

5.3.
The dual product

Let us return to the chain-level product
\pi_{M_{\alpha}}
on the complex
C_{*}(A,M_{\alpha})
, which we defined in
Definition

5.4
purely from the (truncated) pre-CY structure of
A
. By definition, this complex is a cone of maps of Hochschild chain complexes

C_{*}(A,M_{\alpha})=C_{*}(A,A^{\vee})[1-n]\oplus C_{*}(A,A)

with differential combining the Hochschild differentials with the map
F_{\alpha}
induced by the map of bimodules
f_{\alpha}
in (
8
). The product
\pi_{M_{\alpha}}
restricts to a product
\pi
on the subcomplex
C_{*}(A,A)
by construction, but it does not induce a chain operation on the complex
C_{*}(A,A^{\vee})[1-n]
. Note that we always have a pairing

\langle g^{A^{\vee}}(-),-\rangle\colon C_{*}(A,A^{\vee})[-n]\otimes C_{*}(A,A)\to\Bbbk

whose induced pairing on homology is non-degenerate when
\alpha
is non-degenerate. Thus a degree
n
product on
C_{*}(A,A^{\vee})[1-n]
is exactly the type of operation that could be dual to a coproduct of degree
1-n
on
C_{*}(A,A)
. However, recall that the coproduct
\lambda_{H}
we defined in
Section

3.2
only gives a map of complexes after a quotient.

5.3.1.
Homological algebra setup

For the sake of clarity, let us describe a certain algebraic setup in general. Suppose that we have complexes of
\Bbbk
-modules
X,Y
, together with a pairing, that is, a map of complexes

(-,-)\colon X\otimes Y\to\Bbbk

such that the induced map
H_{*}X\to H_{*}(Y)^{\vee}
is
surjective
. Suppose that we also have a subcomplex
W\subseteq Y
such that the induced map
H_{*}(W)\to H_{*}(Y)
is
injective
; as a consequence, the long exact sequence in homology splits into short exact sequences

0\to H_{*}(W)\to H_{*}(Y)\to H_{*}(Y/W)\to 0

which upon dualization give exact sequences

0\to H_{*}(Y/W)^{\vee}\to H_{*}(Y)^{\vee}\to H_{*}(W)^{\vee}

Let us denote
Z_{*}(-)
and
B_{*}(-)
for the cycles and boundaries subcomplexes. We now define a subcomplex of
X

K\coloneqq\{x\in Z_{*}(X)\ |\ \forall w\in Z_{*}(W),(x,w)=0\}\subseteq X.

and pick any subcomplex
Q
of
X
. We note that
B_{*}(X)\subseteq K
.

Lemma 5.13
.

There is a
surjective
map of graded
\Bbbk
-modules
f\colon K/B_{*}(Q)\to H_{*}(Y/W)^{\vee}
making the diagram

\textstyle{K/B_{*}(Q)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{f}
\textstyle{H_{*}(X)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\textstyle{H_{*}(Y/W)^{\vee}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{p^{\vee}}
\textstyle{H_{*}(Y)^{\vee}}

commute.

Proof.

We first note that
K/B_{*}(Q)\to K/B_{*}(X)
is surjective, so it is enough to prove the statement with
Q=X
. Every class in the image of
K/B_{*}(X)\hookrightarrow H_{*}(X)
pairs with zero with the image of
H_{*}(W)\to H_{*}(Y)
, so the map
f
exists by the universal property of the kernel. It also follows that for any
map of sets

s\colon H_{*}(Y/W)\to H_{*}(Y)
giving a section (note that without extra splitness assumptions we do not necessarily have a morphism of graded
\Bbbk
-modules), the pairing

F\colon K/B_{*}(X)\otimes H_{*}(Y/W)\to\Bbbk

corresponding to
f
satisfies
F(a,b)=(i(a),s(b))
. Therefore, given any
\varphi\in H_{*}(Y/W)^{\vee}
, we take
p^{\vee}(\varphi)
, which is a function on
H_{*}(Y/W)
; any function of that form is given by a linear function on
Z_{*}(Y)
satisfying
p^{\vee}(\varphi)(y)=p^{\vee}(\varphi)(y+dz+w)
for all
z\in Y
and
w\in Z_{*}(W)
. But then by assumption of surjectivity of
H_{*}(X)\to H_{*}(Y)^{\vee}
, there exists
x\in Z_{*}(X)
such that
(x,y)=p^{\vee}(\varphi)(y)
for every
y\in Z_{*}(Y)
and by linearity we conclude that
(x,w)=0
for every
w\in Z_{*}(W)
. Thus we must have
x\in K
, and its class in
K/B_{*}(X)
maps to
\varphi
as a function on
H_{*}(Y/W)
, proving surjectivity.
∎

5.3.2.
Lifting the product

To lift the product
\pi_{M_{\alpha}}
to the complex
C_{*}(A,A^{\vee})[1-n]
or to a subcomplex thereof, we use a pair of nullhomotopies of the map of complexes
F_{\alpha}
. In the case where the class of
[F_{\alpha}]
is non-trivial, we can still get a partial lift from a ‘partial nullhomotopy’. Again, let
W
be some subcomplex of
C_{*}(A,A)
such that
H_{*}(W)\to HH_{*}(A,A)
is injective.

Definition 5.14
.

A
homotopy
of
F_{\alpha}
onto
W
is a pair
(E_{0},h)
, where

E_{0}\in W\otimes C_{*}(A,A)\cap C_{*}(A,A)\otimes W,

is closed and
h\colon C_{*}(A,A^{\vee})[-n]\to C_{*}(A,A)[-1]
is a homotopy of maps
C_{*}(A,A^{\vee})[-n]\to C_{*}(A,A)
between
F_{\alpha}
and
{}^{\sharp}E_{0}\circ g^{A^{\vee}}_{\alpha}
.

In other words, since
E_{0}\in C_{*}(A,A)\otimes W
, a partial homotopy as above gives a homotopy between the map
F_{\alpha}
and a map landing in the smaller complex
W
. Given any homotopy as above, we then get a map of graded
\Bbbk
-modules
\iota_{h}\colon C_{*}(A,A^{\vee})[-n+1]\to C_{*}(A,M_{\alpha})
given by
\iota_{h}(x)\coloneqq(x,-h(x))
, where we use the isomorphism of graded
\Bbbk
-modules
C_{*}(A,M_{\alpha})\cong C_{*}(A,A^{\vee})[-n+1]\oplus C_{*}(A,A)
; it follows from the definition above that this map restricts to a
map of complexes

\iota_{h}\colon\ker(^{\sharp}E_{0}\circ g^{A^{\vee}}_{\alpha})\to C_{*}(A,M_{\alpha}).

Proposition 5.15
.

Let
(E_{01},h_{1}),(E_{02},h_{2})
be two homotopies of
F_{\alpha}
onto
W
. Then the map

\pi_{h_{1},h_{2}}(x_{1},x_{2})=p\pi_{M_{\alpha}}(\iota_{h_{1}}(x_{1}),\iota_{h_{2}}(x_{2}))

where
p
is the projection
C_{*}(A,M_{\alpha})[n]\to C_{*}(A,A^{\vee})[-n]
gives a map of complexes

\left(\ker(^{\sharp}E_{01}\circ g^{A^{\vee}}_{\alpha})\otimes C_{*}(A,A^{\vee})[-n+1]\right)\cap\left(C_{*}(A,A^{\vee})[-n+1]\otimes\ker(^{\sharp}E_{02}\circ g^{A^{\vee}}_{\alpha})\right)\to C_{*}(A,A^{\vee})[1],

whose induced map on homology only depends on the
h_{i}
up to
[d,-]
-exact terms.

Let us from now on assume that
A
is connective. Let us denote

Q\coloneqq\ker(^{\sharp}E_{01}\circ g^{A^{\vee}}_{\alpha})\cap\ker(^{\sharp}E_{02}\circ g^{A^{\vee}}_{\alpha})

and apply the construction of
Section

5.3.1
with

X=C_{*}(A,A^{\vee})[-n],\quad Y=C_{*}(A,A),\quad(-,-)=\langle g^{A^{\vee}}_{\alpha}(-),-\rangle,

defining a subcomplex

K\coloneqq\{x\in C_{*}(A,A^{\vee})[-n]\ |\ dx=0\ \text{and}\ \forall w\in W\ \text{such that}\ dw=0,\langle g^{A^{\vee}}_{\alpha}(x),w\rangle=0\}.

Since
E_{01},E_{02}
are closed elements of degree zero in
W\otimes C_{*}(A,A)
and this complex is supported in nonnegative degrees, we have
E_{01},E_{02}\in Z_{0}(W)\otimes Z_{0}(C_{*}(A,A))
, which implies that
K\subseteq Q
. We can then restrict the operation
\pi_{h_{1},h_{2}}
to
K\otimes K
.

Definition 5.16
.

With the same assumptions of
Proposition

5.15
, and assuming
A
connective, we define the
chain-level dual product
to be the map of complexes given by the restriction

\pi_{h_{1},h_{2}}\colon K\otimes K\to C_{*}(A,A^{\vee})[1],

and the
homology dual product
to be the corresponding induced map

\pi_{h_{1},h_{2}}\colon\frac{K}{B_{*}(Q)}\otimes\frac{K}{B_{*}(Q)}\to HH_{*}(A,A^{\vee})[1],

Proposition 5.17
.

The homology dual product
\pi_{h_{1},h_{2}}
only depends on the values of
h_{i}
on
K
up to exact terms, and is
(-1)^{n}
-commutative when
h_{1}-h_{2}
takes exact values on
K
.

Proof.

Follows from the fact that
\pi_{M_{\alpha}}
is a map of complexes which is
(-1)^{n}
-commutative on homology, and from the fact that the maps

\iota_{h_{i}}
are maps of complexes
K[1]\to C_{*}(A,M_{\alpha})
, whose induced map on homology only depends on the values
h_{i}(x)
for
x\in K
up to exact terms.
∎

Definition 5.18
.

The quadruple
(W,h_{1},h_{2},\alpha)
is
balanced
if the image of the chain-level dual product
\pi_{h_{1},h_{2}}
lies in
K
.

When
\Bbbk
is a field and the quadruple
(W,h_{1},h_{2},\alpha)
is balanced, taking homology we get a product

\overline{\pi}_{h_{1},h_{2}}\colon\frac{K}{B_{*}(Q)}[-n]\otimes\frac{K}{B_{*}(Q)}[-n]\to\frac{K}{B_{*}(Q)}[1],

which as a consequence of
Proposition

5.17
is graded commutative when
h_{1}|_{K}
and
h_{2}|_{K}
differ from each other by
[d,-]
-exact terms.

5.3.3.
Associativity of the homology dual product

Asssume that
\Bbbk
is a field and that we made a balanced choice of quadruple
(W,h_{1},h_{2},\alpha)
, so that it makes sense to discuss the associativity properties of
\pi_{h_{1},h_{2}}
.

Proposition 5.19
.

If
A
is smooth over a field
\Bbbk
, connective with a nondegenerate (4-truncated) pre-CY structure of dimension
n\geq 3
, the quadruple
(W,h_{1},h_{2},\alpha)
is balanced and
h_{1}-h_{2}
takes exact values on
K
, then the homology dual product
\overline{\pi}_{h_{1},h_{2}}
on
K/B_{*}(Q)[-n]
is associative.

Proof.

Given any homotopy
h\colon C_{*}(A,A^{\vee})[-n]\to C_{*}(A,A)[-1]
of
F_{\alpha}
, we have a map

\rho_{h}\colon C_{*}(A,M_{\alpha})\to C_{*}(A,A)

given by
\rho_{h}(x,y)=y+h(x)
. By definition, this map satisfies
\rho_{h}\circ\iota_{h}=0
, and also the identity of endomorphisms of
C_{*}(A,M_{\alpha})

\iota_{h}\circ p+\rho_{h}=\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits.

We now take any three elements
x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}
of
K
and use this identity to write

\displaystyle\pi_{h_{1},h_{2}}(\pi_{h_{1},h_{2}}(x_{1},x_{2}),x_{3})

\displaystyle=p\pi_{M_{\alpha}}(\iota_{h_{1}}p\pi_{M_{\alpha}}(\iota_{h_{1}}x_{1},\iota_{h_{2}}x_{2}),\iota_{h_{2}}x_{3})

\displaystyle=p\pi_{M_{\alpha}}(\pi_{M_{\alpha}}(\iota_{h_{1}}x_{1},\iota_{h_{2}}x_{2}),\iota_{h_{2}}x_{3})-p\pi_{M_{\alpha}}(\rho_{h_{1}}\pi_{M_{\alpha}}(\iota_{h_{1}}x_{1},\iota_{h_{2}}x_{2}),\iota_{h_{2}}x_{3})

\displaystyle\pi_{h_{1},h_{2}}(x_{1},\pi_{h_{1},h_{2}}(x_{2},x_{3}))

\displaystyle=p\pi_{M_{\alpha}}(\iota_{h_{1}}x_{1},\iota_{h_{2}}p\pi_{M_{\alpha}}(\iota_{h_{1}}x_{2},\iota_{h_{2}}x_{3}))

\displaystyle=p\pi_{M_{\alpha}}(\iota_{h_{1}}x_{1},\pi_{M_{\alpha}}(\iota_{h_{2}}x_{2},\iota_{h_{2}}x_{3}))-p\pi_{M_{\alpha}}(\iota_{h_{1}}x_{1},\rho_{h_{2}}\pi_{M_{\alpha}}(\iota_{h_{1}}x_{2},\iota_{h_{2}}x_{3}))

We note that every term in the second and fourth line of the equation above only has maps of complexes, so it is enough to prove the desired associativity for the corresponding maps on homology. On homology, the two former terms of those lines are equal since
\iota_{h_{1}}=\iota_{h_{2}}
and
\pi_{M_{\alpha}}
is associative. The two latter terms, involving
\rho_{h_{1}},\rho_{h_{2}}
, should be seen as a defect of associativity, and vanish for degree reasons given our assumptions: since
HH_{*}(A,A)
is supported in nonnegative degrees, so
\rho_{h_{1}},\rho_{h_{2}}
vanish on negative degrees, and
\alpha
is nondegenerate,
HH_{*}(A,A^{\vee})[-n]\cong(\mathop{\mathrm{HH}}\nolimits_{*}(A,A))^{\vee}
is supported in nonpositive degrees so the image of
\pi_{M_{\alpha}}
is concentrated in degrees
(-\infty,2-n]
.
∎

6.
Relations between products on the dual and coproducts

In this section we establish the relation between the dual products
\pi_{h_{1},h_{2}}
, which we got by choosing homotopies of
f_{\alpha}
, and the coproduct
\lambda_{H}
we get by choosing a trivialization
H
of
E
. In the process, we prove a symmetry statement for
[E]
under the non-degeneracy assumption on
\alpha
.

6.1.
Symmetry of Chern character

Recall that in
Definition

3.3
we defined a chain-level Chern character
E\in C_{*}(A,A)\otimes C_{*}(A,A)
given a smooth
A_{\infty}
-category
A
and chain-level representatives for the vertices
\mathop{\mathrm{co}}\nolimits
and
\eta
. Given any
2
-truncated
n
-dimensional pre-CY structure
m=\mu+\alpha
, we can compose both sides of
E
with
g_{\alpha}:C_{*}(A,A)\to C^{*}(A,A)[n]
to get an element of degree
-2n

(\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits\otimes g_{\alpha})(g_{\alpha}\otimes\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits)E\in C^{*}(A,A)\otimes C^{*}(A,A).

We specify the order of application of the
g_{\alpha}
maps due to the possibly nontrivial sign difference
(g_{\alpha}\otimes\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits)(\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits\otimes g_{\alpha})=g_{\alpha}\otimes g_{\alpha}=(-1)^{n}(\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits\otimes g_{\alpha})(g_{\alpha}\otimes\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits)
.

To make the visualization easier, we cut along an arc going from one boundary component of the elbow to the other, and draw the ribbon graphs in the square as follows, namely we identify the bottom edge with the top edge of the square. We insert
\alpha\otimes\alpha
into the circles labeled I and II:

Note that pairing with the right-hand output of
D_{\alpha}
gives a map

(D_{\alpha})^{\sharp}:C_{*}(A,A^{\vee})\to C^{*}(A,A)[2n]

which is
equal at chain-level
to
g_{\alpha}\circ F_{\alpha}
. Besides the chain-level expressions for
\mathop{\mathrm{co}}\nolimits,\eta
, recall from
Section

4.2.1
that we fixed a (non-closed) bimodule morphism
\beta:A\to A
of degree
1
, witnessing the relation between
\mathop{\mathrm{co}}\nolimits,\eta

Lemma 6.1
.

The elements
(\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits\otimes g_{\alpha})(g_{\alpha}\otimes\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits)E
and
D_{\alpha}
are homologous, i.e. there is an explicit element
J_{\alpha}\in C^{*}(A,A)\otimes C^{*}(A,A)
, depending on the chain-level expressions for
\alpha,\mathop{\mathrm{co}}\nolimits,\eta
and
\beta
, satisfying

dJ_{\alpha}=(\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits\otimes g_{\alpha})(g_{\alpha}\otimes\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits)E-D_{\alpha}

Proof.

We write in
Section

A.6.1
an explicit combination of oriented ribbon quivers giving the element
J_{\alpha}
.
∎

Let us denote by
(-)^{T}
the action of the generator of
\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}
permuting the two factors.

Lemma 6.2
.

The elements
D_{\alpha}
and
D_{\alpha}^{T}
are homologous, i.e. there is an explicit element
L_{\alpha}\in C^{*}(A,A)\otimes C^{*}(A,A)
satisfying
dL_{\alpha}=D_{\alpha}-D_{\alpha}^{T}

∎

From the above lemmas, we conclude that the elements
(\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits\otimes g_{\alpha})(g_{\alpha}\otimes\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits)E
and

(g_{\alpha}\otimes\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits)(\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits\otimes g_{\alpha})E^{T}=(-1)^{n}(\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits\otimes g_{\alpha})(g_{\alpha}\otimes\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits)E^{T}

are homologous. Therefore we can conclude a symmetry property of the class
[E]
, in the case that
A
admits a non-degenerate
\alpha
.

Theorem 6.3
.

If the smooth
A_{\infty}
-category
A
admits a nondegenerate (2-truncated) pre-Calabi-Yau structure of dimension
n
, then its class
[E]
is
(-1)^{n}
-symmetric. In particular, over a field
\Bbbk
of characteristic zero, if
A
admits a weak smooth Calabi-Yau structure of dimension
n
, that is, if there is a quasi-isomorphism of bimodules
A\simeq A^{!}[-n]
, then its class
[E]
is
(-1)^{n}
-symmetric.

6.2.
Compatibility relation

We will now study the compatibility between the coproducts
\lambda_{H}
from
Definition

3.7
and the dual products
\pi_{h_{1},h_{2}}
from
Definition

5.16
. This relation will allow us to complete the proof of
Theorem

1.5
. This is the most involved proof in this paper: it involves calculating some rather complicated homotopies, so we will break the proof into parts.

6.2.1.
The square-filling lemma

Let us start with a lemma which holds for any smooth
A
with pre-CY structure, not necessarily nondegenerate. We keep this separate from the main proof since we believe it may be of future interest, e.g., when studying operations coming from a possibly degenerate pre-CY structure.

Recall that
G(\varphi)
gives a homotopy between capping with
\varphi
onto the left factor of
E
and onto the right factor of
E
. Passing to Hochschild cochains using
(\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits\otimes g_{\alpha})(g_{\alpha}\otimes\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits)
, we have a similar description for the cup product. We define

where the two diagrams are taken with orientation
(13\ 12\ \dots\ 1)
and evaluated with
\alpha\otimes\alpha
input into I and II. The map
\Gamma:C^{*}(A,A)\to C^{*}(A,A)\otimes C^{*}(A,A)[2n-1]
then satisfies the equation

d(\Gamma(\varphi))+\Gamma(d\varphi)=((\smile\varphi\otimes\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits)-(\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits\otimes\varphi\smile))(\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits\otimes g_{\alpha})(g_{\alpha}\otimes\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits)E

The element
J_{\alpha}
of
Lemma

6.1
, by cupping on the left or on the right, gives a homotopy between each of the two terms on the right-hand side of the equation above and another term involving cupping with the element
D_{\alpha}
:

\displaystyle d((\smile\varphi\otimes\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits)J_{\alpha})+(\smile d\varphi\otimes\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits)J_{\alpha}

\displaystyle=-(\smile\varphi\otimes\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits)(\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits\otimes g_{\alpha})(g_{\alpha}\otimes\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits)(E)+(\smile\varphi\otimes\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits)D_{\alpha}

\displaystyle d((\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits\otimes\varphi\smile)J_{\alpha})+(\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits\otimes d\varphi\smile)J_{\alpha}

\displaystyle=-(\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits\otimes\varphi\smile)(\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits\otimes g_{\alpha})(g_{\alpha}\otimes\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits)(E)+(\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits\otimes\varphi\smile)D_{\alpha}

We can easily picture another combination of diagrams which gives a homotopy between the two last terms of the equations above, by ‘passing’ the
\varphi
-vertex through the lines of the diagram. Taking
I_{\alpha}
to be the evaluation of the following map on
\alpha\otimes\alpha

we have the equation

dI_{\alpha}(\varphi)+I_{\alpha}(d\varphi)=(\smile\varphi\otimes\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits)D_{\alpha}-(\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits\otimes\varphi\smile)D_{\alpha}

Heuristically, the homotopies above are the
four sides of a square
, which sits inside of some topological space given by the realization of a cell complex, which should be seen as the space of operations on Hochschild (co)chains that we can realize with our calculus, the cells of which are labelled by our oriented diagrams. One can then naturally ask if there is a combination of cells that ‘fills in’ the squares, and the answer is yes:

Lemma 6.4
.

There is a map

N_{\alpha}:C^{*}(A,A)\to C^{*}(A,A)\otimes C^{*}(A,A)[2n-2]

depending on
\alpha
and
\beta
, such that we have an equality in
C^{*}(A,A)\otimes C^{*}(A,A)

dN_{\alpha}(\varphi)-N_{\alpha}(d\varphi)=\Gamma(\varphi)+(\smile\varphi\otimes\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits)J_{\alpha}-(\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits\otimes\varphi\smile)J_{\alpha}-I_{\alpha}(\varphi)

for every
\varphi\in C^{*}(A,A)
.

Proof.

We give an expression for the element
N_{\alpha}
in
Section

A.6.2
.
∎

6.2.2.
The compatibility relation

We return to the setting of
Section

5.3.1
, and consider the map
g_{\alpha}\circ F_{\alpha}\colon C_{*}(A,A^{\vee})[-n]\to C^{*}(A,A)[n]
. Suppose that we are given two elements

E_{01},E_{02}\in W\otimes C_{*}(A,A)\cap C_{*}(A,A)\otimes W

and two maps
\widetilde{h}_{1},\widetilde{h}_{2}\colon C_{*}(A,A^{\vee})[-n]\to C^{*}(A,A)[n-1]
satisfying

[d,\widetilde{h}_{1}]=g_{\alpha}\circ F_{\alpha}-g_{\alpha}\circ^{\sharp}E_{01}\circ g^{A^{\vee}}_{\alpha},\quad[d,\widetilde{h}_{2}]=g_{\alpha}\circ F_{\alpha}-g_{\alpha}\circ^{\sharp}E_{02}\circ g^{A^{\vee}}_{\alpha},

in other words,
\widetilde{h}_{1},\widetilde{h}_{2}
are homotopies between
g_{\alpha}\circ F_{\alpha}
and maps landing in the subcomplex
g_{\alpha}(W)
. We can rewrite the pairing between the dual product and a Hochschild cochain in terms of the
\widetilde{h}_{i}
, by using the following lemma:

Lemma 6.5
.

For any pair
(\widetilde{h}_{1},\widetilde{h}_{2})
as above, if
\alpha
is non-degenerate, there exists a pair of homotopies
(E_{01},h_{1}),(E_{02},h_{2})
of
F_{\alpha}
such that for any closed elements
x_{1},x_{2}\in K
and
\varphi\in C^{*}(A,A)
, there is an equality

\displaystyle\langle\pi_{h_{1},h_{2}}(x_{1},x_{2}),\varphi\rangle

\displaystyle=\Lambda_{\alpha}(x_{1},x_{2},\varphi)-(-1)^{\deg(x_{1})\deg(x_{2})}\langle x_{1},\varphi\smile\widetilde{h}_{2}(x_{2})\rangle

\displaystyle+(-1)^{\deg(x_{2})\deg(\varphi)}\langle x_{2},\varphi\smile\widetilde{h}_{1}(x_{1})\rangle

where
\Lambda_{\alpha}
is a map defined by evaluating a certain combination of oriented ribbon quivers (
Section

A.6.3
) on
\alpha\otimes\alpha
. Moreover, if
\widetilde{h}_{1}
and
\widetilde{h}_{2}
restricted to
K
differ by a
[d,-]
-exact term on
K
, we can also choose
h_{1},h_{2}
whose restriction to
K
differ by a
[d,-]
-exact term.

Proof.

Given in
Section

A.6.3
.
∎

Suppose now that we are given a trivialization
H
of
E
onto
W
. We define:

(9)

\displaystyle\begin{aligned} E_{01}=(-1)^{n}E^{T}_{0},\quad&\widetilde{h}_{1}=\left((\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits\otimes g_{\alpha})(g_{\alpha}\otimes\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits)H+J_{\alpha}+L_{\alpha}\right)^{\sharp}\\
E_{02}=E_{0},\quad&\widetilde{h}_{2}=\ ^{\sharp}\left((\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits\otimes g_{\alpha})(g_{\alpha}\otimes\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits)H+J_{\alpha}\right)\end{aligned}

that is, maps given by pairing either on the right or the left-hand side of the specified elements of
C^{*}(A,A)\otimes C^{*}(A,A)
. Recall we have subcomplexes

K\coloneqq\{x\in C_{*}(A,A^{\vee})[-n]\ |\ dx=0\ \text{and}\ \forall w\in W\ \text{such that}\ dw=0,\langle g^{A^{\vee}}_{\alpha}(x),w\rangle=0\}

and
Q\coloneqq\ker(E_{0}^{\sharp}\circ g^{A^{\vee}}_{\alpha})\cap\ker(^{\sharp}E_{0}\circ g^{A^{\vee}}_{\alpha})
.

Lemma 6.6
.

For any closed elements
x_{1},x_{2}\in K,\ \varphi\in C^{*}(A,A)
, the following equation holds:

\displaystyle(-1)^{\deg(x_{1})\deg(x_{2})}\langle x_{2}\otimes x_{1},(\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits\otimes g_{\alpha})(g_{\alpha}\otimes\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits)\widetilde{\lambda}_{H}(\varphi)\rangle

\displaystyle=\Lambda_{\alpha}(x_{1},x_{2},\varphi)-(-1)^{\deg(x_{1})\deg(x_{2})}\langle x_{1},\varphi\smile\widetilde{h}_{2}(x_{2})\rangle+(-1)^{\deg(x_{2})\deg(\varphi)}\langle x_{2},\varphi\smile\widetilde{h}_{1}(x_{1})\rangle

Proof.

Follows from the definition of
\widetilde{\lambda}_{H},\widetilde{h}_{1},\widetilde{h}_{2}
, together with
Lemma

6.4
and a homotopy that we give at the end of
Section

A.6.3
.
∎

The following proposition follows from
Lemmas

6.6
and
6.5
:

Proposition 6.7
.

Given any trivialization
(E_{0},H)
of
H
onto
W
, if
\alpha
is nondegenerate there are two homotopies
((-1)^{n}E^{T}_{0}h_{1}),(E_{0},h_{2})
of
F_{\alpha}
such that for any closed elements
x_{1},x_{2}\in K
and
y\in C_{*}(A,A)
we have the equation

\langle\pi_{h_{1},h_{2}}(x_{1},x_{2}),g_{\alpha}(y)\rangle=(-1)^{\deg(x_{1})\deg(x_{2})}\langle x_{2}\otimes x_{1},(\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits\otimes g_{\alpha})(g_{\alpha}\otimes\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits)\lambda_{H}(y)\rangle

We note that in the proposition above, we do not make any assumption about the ‘balanced’ condition, or impose any symmetry condition on
H
or
E_{0}
, and that the result holds with any ring
\Bbbk
over which the data
\alpha,H
etc. is defined.

Corollary 6.8
.

If
\Bbbk
is a field, for any choice of homotopies
h_{1},h_{2}
produced by
Proposition

6.7
, the homology loop coproduct

\lambda_{H}\colon HH_{*}(A,A)[n-1]\to\overline{HH}_{*}(A,A)[n-1]\otimes\overline{HH}_{*}(A,A)[n-1]

is entirely determined by the homology dual product

\pi_{h_{1},h_{2}}\colon\frac{K}{B_{*}(Q)}[n]\otimes\frac{K}{B_{*}(Q)}[-n]\to HH_{*}(A,A^{\vee})[1].

Proof.

The pairing we used induces an isomorphism
HH_{*}(A,A^{\vee})[-n]\cong(HH_{*}(A,A))^{\vee}
, and by
Lemma

5.13
also gives a surjective map
\frac{K}{B_{*}(Q)}\to H_{*}(Y/W)^{\vee}
; the result above follows from these two facts together with the equation of
Proposition

6.7
, which holds for all closed elements.
∎

Finally, we relate the two conditions that we called ‘balanced’.

Proposition 6.9
.

If
\Bbbk
is a field, when the triple
(W,H,\alpha)
is balanced, in the sense of
Definition

3.9
, then any quadruple
(W,h_{1},h_{2},\alpha)
from
Proposition

6.7
is balanced, in the sense of
Definition

5.18
.

Proof.

Recall that
(W,H,\alpha)
is balanced if the image of
W
under
\lambda_{H}
is contained in
W\otimes C_{*}(A,A)\cap C_{*}(A,A)\otimes W
. Over a field we have

H_{*}(W\otimes C_{*}(A,A)\cap C_{*}(A,A)\otimes W)\cong H_{*}(W\otimes W)\cong H_{*}(W)\otimes H_{*}(W)

so for
[y]\in HH_{*}(A,A)
, we can represent
\lambda(y)
by a linear combination of pairs of closed elements of
W
. Thus, applying the equation in
Proposition

6.7
, we conclude that for
x_{1},x_{2}\in K
we have
\pi_{h_{1},h_{2}}(x_{1},x_{2})\in K
.
∎

Remark 6.10
.

If
\lambda_{H}
happens to be defined over some ring
\Bbbk
, the equation of
Proposition

6.7
still holds at chain-level, but it may be that the homology coproduct
\lambda_{H}
contain
more information
than the dual coproduct. This is expected, since we lose all the information about torsion classes by taking linear duals. We present an example of this fact in
Section

7.2.6
.

6.2.3.
Symmetry of
H

Note that the statement of
Proposition

6.7
does not depend on any symmetry conditions on
H
. Recall that we have
dH=E-E_{0}
, and
E_{0}
is
(-1)^{n}
-symmetric by assumption.

We know from
Lemmas

6.1
and
6.2
that upon applying
g_{\alpha}
on both sides, we have an explicit relation between
E
and its transpose:

d(J_{\alpha}+L_{\alpha}-J_{\alpha}^{T})=(\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits\otimes g_{\alpha})(g_{\alpha}\otimes\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits)(E-(-1)^{n}E^{T})

Therefore it is natural to consider the following symmetry condition on the complex where
H
lives.

Definition 6.11
.

A (partial) trivialization
H
of
E
is
\alpha
-symmetric
modulo closed terms in
W
if the expression

(\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits\otimes g_{\alpha})(g_{\alpha}\otimes\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits)(H-(-1)^{n}H^{T})+J_{\alpha}+L_{\alpha}-J_{\alpha}^{T}

is exact in
C^{*}(A,A)\otimes C^{*}(A,A)
modulo terms in
g_{\alpha}(Z_{*}(W))\otimes g_{\alpha}(Z_{*}(W))
.

Proposition 6.12
.

If
H
is
\alpha
-symmetric modulo closed terms in
W
, then
h_{1}
and
h_{2}
in
Proposition

6.7
can be chosen so that their values on
K
differ by exact terms.

Proof.

The element
H
being
\alpha
-symmetric modulo closed terms in
W
implies that there exists
\Phi\in C^{*}(A,A)\otimes C^{*}(A,A)
such that

d\Phi=(\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits\otimes g_{\alpha})(g_{\alpha}\otimes\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits)(H-(-1)^{n}H^{T})+J_{\alpha}+L_{\alpha}-J_{\alpha}^{T}+X

where
X\in g_{\alpha}(Z_{*}(W))\otimes g_{\alpha}(Z_{*}(W))
. Thus
\widetilde{h}_{1}
and
\widetilde{h}_{2}
in
Eq.

9
will differ on
K
by exact values. Then the result follows from the second assertion of
Lemma

6.5
.
∎

Theorem 6.13
.

Let
\Bbbk
be a field. If
H
is
\alpha
-symmetric modulo closed terms in
W
, then the coproduct
\overline{\lambda}_{H}
is
(-1)^{n}
-cocommutative at the homology level. If moreover
A
is connective and
n\geq 3
, then it is also coassociative at the homology level.

Proof.

Combining
Propositions

6.12
,
5.17
and
5.19
, we obtain that the homology dual product
\overline{\pi}_{H}\coloneqq\pi_{h_{1},h_{2}}
is
(-1)^{n}
-commutative, and associative if
A
is connective and
n\geq 3
. The result then follows from the fact that the space
K/B_{*}(Q)
on which this dual product is defined surjects onto
\overline{HH}_{*}(A,A)^{\vee}
, so we can deduce cocommutativity and coassociativity of
\overline{\lambda}_{H}
from the dual properties on
\overline{\pi}_{H}
.
∎

The results above are what we stated in the Introduction as
Theorem

1.5
. We conclude this section by making a remark. The condition of being
\alpha
-symmetric modulo closed terms in
W
stated in
Definition

6.11
requires the term in question to be exact modulo something in
g_{\alpha}(Z_{*}(W))\otimes g_{\alpha}(Z_{*}(W))
, instead of just modulo something in the larger subcomplex

g_{\alpha}(W)\otimes C^{*}(A,A)\cap C^{*}(A,A)\otimes g_{\alpha}(W).

This may seem excessive, as the value of the coproduct
\lambda_{H}
is invariant under changes in
H
by terms in the complex
W\otimes C_{*}(A,A)\cap C_{*}(A,A)\otimes W
, but it is necessary to prove our theorem since elements in
K
are only required to vanish on closed elements of
W
. However, it turns out that this distinction is irrelevant when
\Bbbk
is a field of characteristic
\neq 2
, in which case one can state the following variant.

Definition 6.14
.

Over a field
\Bbbk
of characteristic
\neq 2
, we say that a (partial) trivialization
H
of
E
is
\alpha
-symmetric
modulo
W
if

(\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits\otimes g_{\alpha})(g_{\alpha}\otimes\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits)(H-(-1)^{n}H^{T})+J_{\alpha}+L_{\alpha}-J_{\alpha}^{T}

is exact in
C^{*}(A,A)\otimes C^{*}(A,A)/g_{\alpha}(W)\otimes g_{\alpha}(W)
.

The following proposition says that the definition above is as good as
Definition

6.11
for our purposes.

Proposition 6.15
.

Over a field
\Bbbk
of characteristic
\neq 2
, if
H
is
\alpha
-symmetric modulo
W
(in the sense of
Definition

6.14
), then there exists some
\widehat{H}
which is
\alpha
-symmetric modulo closed terms in
W
(in the sense of
Definition

6.11
) and such that
\widehat{H}-H\in W\otimes W
. Therefore
Theorem

6.13
holds also for
H
.

Proof.

Given our assumptions, there exists
X\in W\otimes W
such that

(\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits\otimes g_{\alpha})(g_{\alpha}\otimes\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits)(H-(-1)^{n}H^{T})+J_{\alpha}+L_{\alpha}-J_{\alpha}^{T}=\text{exact}\ +(\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits\otimes g_{\alpha})(g_{\alpha}\otimes\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits)X,

so applying the differential we have

d(\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits\otimes g_{\alpha})(g_{\alpha}\otimes\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits)X=-(\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits\otimes g_{\alpha})(g_{\alpha}\otimes\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits)(E_{0}-(-1)^{n}E_{0}^{T}).

Taking
\widehat{H}=H-X/2
(which makes sense since we can divide by two) we get

(\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits\otimes g_{\alpha})(g_{\alpha}\otimes\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits)(\widehat{H}-(-1)^{n}\widehat{H}^{T})+J_{\alpha}+L_{\alpha}-J_{\alpha}^{T}=\text{exact}\ +(\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits\otimes g_{\alpha})(g_{\alpha}\otimes\mathop{\mathrm{id}}\nolimits)\frac{X+(-1)^{n}X^{T}}{2},

whose last term is closed and therefore by Künneth it is homologous to something in
g_{\alpha}(Z_{*}(W))\otimes g_{\alpha}(Z_{*}(W))
.
∎

7.
Examples

The formalism of pre-CY structures and the associated calculus developed in
[
KTV21
]
is suitable for constructing homotopies and higher structures described in terms of diagrams. Evaluating such diagrams involves taking sums over many expressions, which is often impractical. However, in particular examples, one can perform explicit calculations by hand. We would like to present some of these calculations using examples of interest for string topology.

In this section we will study the algebraic loop product and coproduct for algebras given by the homology of the loop spaces of spheres. Spheres are formal and coformal
[
Ber14
,
BB17
]
, so the graded algebra
A=H_{*}(\Omega S^{N},\Bbbk)
is quasi-isomorphic to the dg algebra of chains on
\Omega S^{N}
. We reiterate that, for some general manifold
M
, this homology will not be quasi-isomorphic to the algebra of chains, so looking at the homology algebra
H_{*}(\Omega M)
would not give the correct answers.

One should be careful when comparing the calculations we perform below to the geometric loop coproduct, since the algebraic operation
\lambda_{H}
we defined
is not invariant
with respect to quasi-isomorphisms of
A
. In fact, for some choices of
H
,
\lambda_{H}
might not have a geometric interpretation and the space of “geometrically meaningful” trivializations seems to be more restricted.

Still, we believe that the examples we calculate below could be of interest for string topology. It may seem like this chain-level formalism is overly complicated for calculating such simple examples; nevertheless, we argue that it allows for a systematic treatment of signs which, in some cases, as for the even-dimensional spheres
Section

7.2
, allows us to work over
\mathbb{Z}
and understand the behavior of torsion classes.

The cases of the circle and the 2-sphere are of particular interest; in both of those cases, there are multiple choices of
\alpha
-symmetric (
Definition

6.11
) trivialization
H
, some of which give non-coassociative coproducts
\lambda_{H}
. These examples show that the condition
n\geq 3
in
Theorem

6.13
is necessary.

7.1.
Spheres of odd dimension greater or equal to 3

Let us take
A=\Bbbk[t],\deg(t)=2N\geq 2
, seen as a homologically graded dg algebra over
\Bbbk
with trivial differential. As mentioned above, this is the homology algebra of
\Omega S^{2N+1}
, and since the sphere is coformal, the Hochschild homology of
A
calculates the homology of
LS^{2N+1}
. More explicitly, it is given by

HH_{*}(A,A)=\Bbbk\ \bigoplus_{k\geq 1}\ (\Bbbk[2Nk]\oplus\Bbbk[2Nk+1])

This may be computed using the Koszul resolution of
A
in
Eq.

10
below, and we may pick some simple representatives in the Hochschild chain complex
C_{*}(A,A)
(see
Section

2.1.1
) for each of those classes: the chain of length one
t^{k}
for the generator in degree
2Nk
, for each
k\geq 0
, and the chain of length two
t^{k-1}[t]
for the generator in degree
2Nk+1
, for each
k\geq 1
. Here,
[t]\in\mathop{\overline{A}}\nolimits[1]
.

Let us also calculate and pick explicit representatives for the non trivial classes in the Hochschild cohomology of
A
. Following the noncommutative geometry analogy between Hochschild cochains and vector fields, we think of
A
as functions on some space with coordinates
s_{k},k\geq 0
, where
s_{k}
is dual to
t^{k}
, and denote by
s_{k_{1}}s_{k_{2}}\dots s_{k_{p}}\partial^{k}
the Hochschild cochain of length
p
that sends the basis element
[t^{k_{1}}]\otimes[t^{k_{2}}]\otimes\dots\otimes[t^{k_{p}}]
to
t^{k}
and all other basis elements
[t^{k_{1}^{\prime}}]\otimes\dots\otimes[t^{k_{q}^{\prime}}]
to zero. We note that for any
k\geq 0
, the cochain
\partial^{k}
of length zero and degree
2Nk
is closed, and so is the cochain
\sum_{i}is_{i}\partial^{i+k}
, of length one and degree
2Nk+1
. It turns out that these are all the representatives for the nonzero Hochschild cohomology classes. We summarize our chosen representatives below:

\hskip-14.22636pt\begin{array}[]{|c||c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline\cr\text{chains}&\dots&t^{2}[t]&t^{3}&t[t]&t^{2}&1[t]&t&1\\
\hline\cr\text{deg in\ }HH_{*}(A,A)&\dots&6N+1&6N&4N+1&4N&2N+1&2N&0\\
\hline\cr\hline\cr\text{cochains}&\dots&\partial^{2}&\sum_{i}is_{i}\partial^{i+2}&\partial^{1}&\sum_{i}is_{i}\partial^{i+1}&\partial^{0}&\sum_{i}is_{i}\partial^{i}&\sum_{i}is_{i}\partial^{i-1}\\
\hline\cr\text{deg in\ }HH^{*}(A,A)&\dots&4N&4N-1&2N&2N-1&0&-1&-2N-1\\
\hline\cr\end{array}

7.1.1.
Chain-level Chern character

Recall that even before we pick any notion of orientation on
A
(smooth CY or pre-CY structure), once we pick chain-level representatives for the canonical vertices
\mathop{\mathrm{co}}\nolimits
and
\eta
we can define the chain-level Chern character of the diagonal bimodule
E
and the operation
G:C^{*}(A,A)\to C_{*}(A,A)\otimes C_{*}(A,A)[-1]
.

First, we must choose an explicit representative for the bimodule dual
A^{!}
. For that, we use the following resolution for the diagonal bimodule
A
:

(10)

\displaystyle\widetilde{A}=(A^{e}[2N+1]\oplus A^{e},d_{\widetilde{A}})

with differential that sends elements of the first summand to the second summand by

d_{\widetilde{A}}(t^{k}\otimes t^{\ell})=t^{k+1}\otimes t^{\ell}-t^{k}\otimes t^{\ell+1}

that is, sending the generator
1\otimes 1\in A^{e}[2N+1]
to
t\otimes 1-1\otimes t\in A^{e}
. We then dualize this bimodule to get a representative of
A^{!}
given by

A^{!}=(A^{e}\oplus A^{e}[-2N-1],d_{A^{!}}).

Let us denote the elements of the first and second summand by
R^{k,\ell},S^{k,\ell}
, respectively (denoting
t^{k}\otimes t^{\ell}
in each factor), with differential given by

d_{A^{!}}(R^{k,\ell})=S^{k+1,\ell}-S^{k,\ell+1}

The bimodule structure is given by the structure maps

\displaystyle\mu(t^{i},R^{k,\ell})

\displaystyle=R^{k+i,\ell}

\displaystyle\mu(R^{k,\ell},t^{i})

\displaystyle=R^{k,\ell+i}

\displaystyle\mu(t^{i},S^{k,\ell})

\displaystyle=S^{k+1,\ell}

\displaystyle\mu(S^{k,\ell},t^{i})

\displaystyle=-S^{k,\ell+i}

We must now find chain-level representatives for the
\mathop{\mathrm{co}}\nolimits
and
\eta
vertices. These are not unique, but we can easily find a choice that satisfies the necessary conditions. For the coevaluation
\mathop{\mathrm{co}}\nolimits\in A\otimes^{\mathbb{L}}_{A^{e}}A^{!}
, we have

(11)

\displaystyle\mathop{\mathrm{co}}\nolimits=1\otimes[\varnothing]\otimes R^{0,0}\otimes[\varnothing]-1\otimes[t]\otimes S^{0,0}\otimes[\varnothing]-1\otimes[\varnothing]\otimes S^{0,0}\otimes[t].

Here,
\mathop{\mathrm{co}}\nolimits
lies in
\bigoplus_{i,j\geq 0}A\otimes\mathop{\overline{A}}\nolimits^{\otimes i}\otimes A^{!}\otimes\mathop{\overline{A}}\nolimits^{\otimes j}
and is illustrated as follows, compare

We check that this element is closed and satisfies the universal property of coevaluation.

For the vertex
\eta
we can then pick the form given by

\eta
t^{n}
R^{k,\ell}

\displaystyle=\eta(t^{n}\otimes R^{k,\ell})=t^{\ell}\otimes t^{n+k}

\eta
[t^{m}]
t^{n}
S^{k,\ell}

\displaystyle=\eta([t^{m}]\otimes t^{n}\otimes S^{k,\ell})=-\sum_{1\leq i\leq m}t^{\ell+i-1}\otimes t^{k+n+m-i}

with all other terms of
\eta
being zero. The first term, involving
R^{k,\ell}
, guarantees that
\eta
and
\mathop{\mathrm{co}}\nolimits
satisfy the required compatibility
Eq.

6
, and the second term, involving
S^{k,\ell}
, makes
\eta
closed under taking the necklace bracket with
\mu
.

Using the vertices above we compute the chain-level Euler character to be
E=0
, since it is a difference between two equal terms
1\otimes 1
, one obtained from pairing the first term of
\mathop{\mathrm{co}}\nolimits
with the first term of
\eta
and the other from pairing the third term of
\mathop{\mathrm{co}}\nolimits
with the second term of
\eta
; all other terms in the evaluation of the diagram are zero. Having
E=0
is obviously expected since the Euler characteristic of
S^{2N+1}
is zero, and the differential on Hochschild chains vanishes in degree one since
A
is commutative.

7.1.2.
The map
G

Since
E=0
at chain-level as explained above, the map
G
is a map of complexes (see
Eq.

7
), and induces a map in cohomology

G\colon HH^{*}(A,A)\to HH_{*}(A,A)\otimes HH_{*}(A,A)[-1].

Let us calculate the chain-level map on
\varphi
ranging over the representatives we picked for the nonzero cohomology classes. We note that the only nonzero diagram to evaluate in the expression for
G(\varphi)
is the term

\mathop{\mathrm{co}}\nolimits
\varphi
\eta
e_{1}
e_{2}
e_{3}
e_{4}
e_{5}

with orientation
(e_{5}\ e_{4}\ e_{3}\ e_{2}\ e_{1})
. We plug in the expressions we picked for
\mathop{\mathrm{co}}\nolimits
and
\eta
, and calculate:

\displaystyle G(\partial_{k})

\displaystyle=\sum_{1\leq i\leq k}(t^{i-1}\otimes t^{k-i}[t]-t^{i-1}[t]\otimes t^{k-i})

\displaystyle G(\sum_{i}is_{i}\partial^{i+k})

\displaystyle=-\sum_{1\leq j\leq k+1}(t^{j-1}\otimes t^{k+1-j})

To calculate the second line above, note that
\mathop{\mathrm{co}}\nolimits
only contains terms with power of
t
equal to one (see
Eq.

11
) so only the term
G(s_{1}\partial^{1+k})
is nonzero.

The map induced by
G
on cohomology does not depend on our choice of
\mathop{\mathrm{co}}\nolimits
and
\eta
; by the discussion in
Section

3.3
, we could compensate a change in the chain-level expressions for those vertices by a change in
H
, but the space of choices for
H
(i.e. the
HH_{0}(A,A)\otimes HH_{1}(A,A)\oplus HH_{1}(A,A)\otimes HH_{0}(A,A)
-torsor) is trivial in homology.

7.1.3.
The CY and pre-CY structures

Let us now pick the orientation on
A
, which for us will be a non-degenerate pre-CY structure. We will prove nondegeneracy by first giving a compatible smooth CY structure:

Proposition 7.1
.

The Hochschild chain
\omega=1[t]\in C_{2N+1}(A,A)
is non-degenerate.

Proof.

We will prove this by explicitly giving its inverse pre-CY structure. Let
\alpha\in C^{2N+1}_{(2)}(A)
be given by the formulas

\alpha
t^{k}
\alpha(\varnothing,t^{k})^{\prime}
\alpha(\varnothing,t^{k})^{\prime\prime}

\displaystyle\qquad\alpha(\varnothing,t^{k})^{\prime}\otimes\alpha(\varnothing,t^{k})^{\prime\prime}=\sum_{0\leq i\leq k-1}t^{i}\otimes t^{k-1-i}

\alpha
t^{k}
\alpha(t^{k},\varnothing)^{\prime}
\alpha(t^{k},\varnothing)^{\prime\prime}

\displaystyle\qquad\alpha(t^{k},\varnothing)^{\prime}\otimes\alpha(t^{k},\varnothing)^{\prime\prime}=-\sum_{0\leq i\leq k-1}t^{i}\otimes t^{k-1-i}

with all other components of
\alpha
being zero. Let us explain this better;
\alpha
only evaluates non-trivially on exactly one input, sending
t^{k}
to the tensor
\pm\sum t^{i}\otimes t^{k-1-i}
, with sign depending on which side this input is on; recall that since the CY dimension is odd,
\alpha
needs to be antisymmetric under the rotation. We can check that this is a closed element of
C^{*}_{(2)}(A)
, under the differential given by taking necklace bracket with the Hochschild cochain giving the
A_{\infty}
structure
\mu
(in this case just the multiplication). In this case this means explicitly verifying the following equation

\lxSVG@closescope {{
{}{}{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{{}}}}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}

for all
k,\ell\geq 0
, which holds since both sides are equal to
-\sum_{0\leq i\leq k+\ell-1}t^{i}\otimes t^{k+\ell-1-i}
.

It remains to check that
\alpha
is indeed an inverse to
\omega
, that is, that the Hochschild cochain given by

\alpha
\omega

is cohomologous to the unit cochain; in this case one can calculate that it is exactly equal to the unit cochain.
∎

In order to apply our results, we need the element
\alpha
we found above to be part of a pre-CY structure. In this case, there is no more trivial terms.

Proposition 7.2
.

Taking
m=\mu+\alpha,m_{(\geq 3)}=0
, gives a pre-CY structure of dimension
2N+1
on
A
.

Proof.

We already verified that
[\mu,\alpha]=0
, so the only equation left to verify is that
[\alpha,\alpha]=0
in
C^{*}_{(3)}(A)
. Since
\alpha
is only nonzero evaluated on exactly one input, the only possibly nontrivial term in
[\alpha,\alpha]
can be on exactly one input. By symmetry it is enough to place it in the first of the three angles; we then have that the only nontrivial terms are

\displaystyle[\alpha,\alpha](t^{k},\varnothing,\varnothing)
